query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The mechanical-property differences in equiatomic FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys are primarily governed by the magnitude of composition-induced local lattice distortions (as measured by MSAD) and the differential solute effects of Cr, Mn, and Fe. Cr increases overall lattice distortion and thereby raises the extrapolated 0 K CRSS, while increased Mn and Fe promote dynamic solute pinning at elevated temperatures that produces a Portevin–Le Chatelier (PL) effect with serrated stress–strain flow.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, water-quenched, equiatomic FCC single crystals of quinary, quaternary, and ternary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys prepared by Bridgman or optical floating-zone methods and annealed for 168 h at 1273 or 1473 K.
generation.intervention: Compression of [1̄23]-oriented single crystals over a temperature range from cryogenic (9 K) to high temperatures (up to 1373 K), combined with strain-rate jump tests, TEM characterization of dislocation structures, and DFT calculations to determine MSAD.
generation.conditions: Tests performed in compression at an engineering strain rate of 1 × 10^-4 s^-1; strain-rate jumps (1 × 10^-4 to 1 × 10^-2 s^-1) applied during low-hardening Stage I (approx. 10% plastic strain); CRSS data fitted excluding regions affected by low-temperature inertial effects and high-temperature PL behavior (above about 873 K).
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions quantified by MSAD, which vary with alloy composition—especially the presence or absence of Cr—and the formation of diffusible Mn- and Fe-rich solute atmospheres that interact elastically with moving dislocations.
generation.mechanism: At temperatures below room temperature, dislocation glide is controlled by thermal activation over solute obstacles, with Cr-induced lattice distortion increasing the dislocation glide resistance. Below ~77 K, inertial effects reduce the steepness of the CRSS increase. At elevated temperatures (above roughly 673–873 K), diffusible Mn- and Fe-rich solutes dynamically pin dislocations via a Cottrell-type elastic interaction, leading to serrated flow (PL effect) and a modest CRSS increase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a room-temperature baseline, alloys richer in Cr will show higher extrapolated 0 K CRSS due to increased local lattice distortion. Conversely, alloys with greater Mn and Fe will exhibit a larger PL-induced CRSS increment and more pronounced serrated plastic flow at high temperatures. At cryogenic temperatures, CRSS will increase steeply compared to room temperature, with the increase tapering off near 77 K due to inertial effects.
generation.baseline: The room-temperature CRSS for equiatomic quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys, and intermediate-temperature CRSS before the onset of PL flow, serve as the baseline for comparing low-temperature inertial and high-temperature solute-pin strengthening effects.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to equiatomic FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based quinary, quaternary, and ternary concentrated solid solutions tested as [1̄23]-oriented bulk single crystals. It holds for deformation in compression within the temperature regimes where conventional thermal activation governs (except below ~60–77 K, where inertial effects dominate) and up to temperatures where dynamic solute effects (PL) become significant (approximately above 673 K).
generation.uncertainty: While the role of local lattice distortion (MSAD) appears robust, the precise quantitative contributions of Agnostic dislocation inertia versus elastic solute–dislocation interactions, and the potential contributions from other microstructural factors (such as magnetic transitions not captured in 0 K DFT), remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform systematic temperature-dependent compression tests on a series of single crystals of equiatomic FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys. Measure the CRSS across a wide temperature range (from ~9 K to 1373 K) while conducting strain-rate jump experiments to delineate inertial effects and the onset of PL flow. Conduct TEM characterization to evaluate dislocation core structures and partial widths, and correlate the extrapolated 0 K CRSS with independently determined MSAD values from DFT.
measurements: CRSS from 0.2% offset yield stresses at varying temperatures
Strain-rate sensitivity and activation volume from strain-rate jump tests
Observation of serrated stress–strain flow (indicative of PL effect) at high temperatures
TEM measurements of partial-dislocation dissociation widths and stacking-fault energies
Correlation of extrapolated τ0/μ with sqrt(MSAD)/b from DFT calculations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with higher Cr content do not exhibit significantly higher extrapolated 0 K CRSS, and if alloys with increased Mn and Fe fail to show a corresponding increase in the high-temperature CRSS increment and serrated flow behavior, then the hypothesis that local lattice distortion and dynamic solute pinning govern the deformation behavior is rejected.
